column4: The section reads 91:9's “aflaha” as lasting in good through purification; 87:14 repeats the pairing directly: “قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ.”
The section's remembered one who fears is named here: “سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَن يَخْشَىٰ”; fear makes the addressee receptive to the reminder.
The section's “ashqa” avoids the reminder here, “وَيَتَجَنَّبُهَا الْأَشْقَىٰ,” the opposite response to the fearful rememberer of 87:10.
“فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ الذِّكْرَىٰ” sets up the division the section quotes in 87:10–11: reminder benefits one who fears, while the most wretched avoids it.
The next ayah gives the consequence of the “ashqa” who avoids the reminder in 87:11: he enters “النَّارَ الْكُبْرَىٰ”; the section's link between wretchedness and a failed end gains its outcome.
After the purified one in 87:14, “وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّىٰ” shows remembering God and prayer as the next concrete response associated with that success.
The people “تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا” choose the near life, a specific counterpoint to the section's reading of success as remaining in good.
“الْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ” states that the better good endures, closely matching the section's lexical gloss of falah as remaining in good.
“إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ” explicitly divides human endeavors; this is the two searches whose different outcomes the section describes.
The good course begins with giving and God-consciousness, “أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ,” concrete deeds leading toward the section's successful outcome.
The good course also affirms “الْحُسْنَىٰ”; that trust in the good corresponds to the section's one who reaches and remains in good.
“فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ” names the eased outcome of that course, a specific result for one of the divergent endeavors in 92:4.
The counter-course is “بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَىٰ,” withholding and acting self-sufficient; it illuminates the section's self whose share is made small.
“وَكَذَّبَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ” makes denial of the good the opposite of the successful, purified course.
The other course is eased toward “الْعُسْرَىٰ,” an explicit adverse result for the seeker who withholds and denies.
The following verse says “مَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ” when he falls; wealth cannot deliver the seeker from the failed end described in 92:8–10.
“نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ” is the fire warned of immediately before 92:15 identifies the most wretched as its entrant, joining that root to a concrete end.
The cited “الْأَشْقَىٰ” enters the blazing fire; it repeats the section's root for the most wretched and connects it to the failed outcome.
“كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ” describes denial and turning away, a concrete counterpart to the avoider of the reminder in 87:11.
“The most God-fearing” is kept away from the fire in “وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا الْأَتْقَىٰ,” the explicit opposite of the ashqa in 92:15.
“يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ يَتَزَكَّىٰ” directly joins giving to purification, matching the section's successful self-purification.
The purifier “لَا يُرِيدُ جَزَاءً” from anyone; this clarifies the self-directed purification in 35:18 that the section cites.
His aim is “ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَىٰ,” giving the searcher in this passage a stated object of pursuit.
“وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ” supplies the sought one's final satisfaction, a concrete counterpart to reaching the desired in the section's gloss of aflaha.
“فَمِنْهُمْ شَقِيٌّ وَسَعِيدٌ” divides people at the final reckoning into wretched and happy, the same opposed outcomes named by the section's root sh-q-w.
The condemned say “غَلَبَتْ عَلَيْنَا شِقْوَتُنَا”; wretchedness has overcome them, giving the section's “ashqa” a first-person account of failure.
Zakariyya says he has never been “شَقِيًّا” in calling on God: here the root means disappointed, a direct reversal of the section's hand left empty.
Jesus says he was not made “جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا”; the paired tyrant and wretchedness recalls 14:15's tyrant who fails, but here is explicitly denied of Jesus.
The Qur'an was not sent “لِتَشْقَىٰ”; this negated use of the section's sh-q-w root distinguishes divine reminder from the toil that ends in wretchedness.
The continuation calls the Qur'an “تَذْكِرَةً لِّمَن يَخْشَىٰ,” specifying the fearful recipient of the reminder after 20:2 denies that it was sent to cause distress.
Moses warns the magicians that “وَقَدْ خَابَ مَنِ افْتَرَىٰ”; the same kh-y-b verb marks false invention as an effort that ends empty.
In the same contest, “لَا يُفْلِحُ السَّاحِرُ” says the magician does not prosper; its outcome repeats the failure tied to falsehood in 20:61.
“وَقَدْ خَابَ مَنْ حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا” repeats the section's khāba formula for one who carries wrongdoing and fails.
“وَخَابَ كُلُّ جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ” directly applies khāba to every defiant tyrant, the same failed outcome named in the section.
God warns Adam that Satan must not expel the pair from the Garden “فَتَشْقَىٰ”; the section's sh-q-w root here names the toil or hardship of the lost garden.
The next ayah describes the Garden's protection from hunger and nakedness, “أَلَّا تَجُوعَ فِيهَا وَلَا تَعْرَىٰ,” making concrete the deprivation behind the warning in 20:117.
Its continuation adds no thirst or sun exposure, “لَا تَظْمَأُ فِيهَا وَلَا تَضْحَىٰ”; these bodily hardships spell out the toil contrasted with the Garden.
After the descent from the Garden, one who follows God's guidance “فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ”; guidance avoids the very wretchedness named in the section.
The next ayah gives the counter-outcome for turning from remembrance: “مَعِيشَةً ضَنكًا,” a constricted life, linking avoidance to a diminished share.

The dictionary form behind the section's “dassā” is literal concealment: “يَدُسُّهُ فِي التُّرَابِ,” burying the newborn girl in dust; it makes the section's hidden-self image tangible while showing its destructive form.
The preceding ayah says the father hides from the people after the news of a daughter; that concealment sets up the literal burial “يَدُسُّهُ” in 16:59.
The cited “وَمَن تَزَكَّىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِ” says purification benefits the purifier; the same ayah says no burdened soul can transfer its load, defining what each person receives.
The thirsty person expects water in a mirage but “إِذَا جَاءَهُ لَمْ يَجِدْهُ شَيْئًا”; this is a specific search that reaches its object and finds nothing, like the section's khāba.
“وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ” ties what a person receives to his own striving, directly clarifying the section's two searches.
The continuation says “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ”; the seeker's own effort is brought into view, not lost from the account.
The next verse promises “ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ,” completing the sequence from striving to its full result.
The command to seek a means toward God and strive, “وَابْتَغُوا إِلَيْهِ الْوَسِيلَةَ وَجَاهِدُوا,” ends “لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ”; it states an aim and effort that lead to success.
“قَدْ أَفْلَحَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ” gives the successful group whose qualities, including doing zakat in 23:4, make the section's success-through-purification concrete.
The successful believers are described as “لِلزَّكَاةِ فَاعِلُونَ”; the root of purification is made an actual deed within their profile.
Those “يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ” are called successful; guarding the self from its grasping disposition contrasts with the section's soul whose share is diminished.
This verse again links success to being protected from “شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ”; it makes the soul's disposition and its outcome explicit, as in the section's self that is purified or suppressed.
The one who “نَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ” restrains the self from desire, a specific opposite to dimming or debasing the self in 91:10.
The next verse names that restrained person's refuge as the Garden, completing the opposed outcome to the section's failed, diminished self.
“عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ” portrays faces laboring and exhausted, closely matching the section's dictionary note that wretchedness is a form of toil.
The exhausted faces in 88:3 “تَصْلَىٰ نَارًا حَامِيَةً”; this gives their toil the ruinous destination described in the section's account of the ashqa.
The same scene continues with drink from “عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ,” an affliction after the exhausted labor of 88:3.
Their food is only “مِن ضَرِيعٍ,” continuing the deprivation that makes this an image of effort ending without benefit.
That food “لَا يُسْمِنُ وَلَا يُغْنِي مِن جُوعٍ”; the laboring person's provision does not satisfy, a concrete empty return.
The next group has “وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاعِمَةٌ,” a direct opposite to the exhausted faces of 88:3.
Their state is “لِسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ,” satisfied with its endeavor, a sharp reversal of the section's labor whose outcome is failure.
The satisfied group's destination is “جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ,” completing the contrast between spent labor and a good attained.
“الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ” are better and more lasting than worldly adornment, closely echoing the section's gloss of falah as remaining in good.
“وَمَن يُجَاهِدُ فَإِنَّمَا يُجَاهِدُ لِنَفْسِهِ” says striving accrues to the striver, a close parallel to the section's account of what each self gains.
This verse states that whoever does good does it “فَلِنَفْسِهِ” and whoever does evil does it against himself, specifying the personal share at stake in the section.
After his garden is ruined, its owner “يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ” over what he spent; the turned palms make wasted expenditure visible, like the section's empty-handed khāba.
The deeds of the wrongdoers are “كَرَمَادٍ اشْتَدَّتْ بِهِ الرِّيحُ,” ashes scattered by wind with no gain from what was earned, an image of effort yielding nothing.

The fire kindled by the hypocrites does light its surroundings, but its light is then taken away: “اسْتَوْقَدَ نَارًا” and “ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ” contrast with the section's fire-striker that never sparks.
God makes fire from a green tree “فَإِذَا أَنتُم مِّنْهُ تُوقِدُونَ,” a successful ignition opposite to the “hayyāb” stick that gives no spark.
The question “أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ” names fire that people kindle, directly reversing the section's fire-making attempt that yields no spark.
The next ayah asks who created the fire's tree, “أَأَنتُمْ أَنشَأْتُمْ شَجَرَتَهَا,” extending the scene from kindling to the source of its fuel.
The fire is made “تَذْكِرَةً وَمَتَاعًا لِّلْمُقْوِينَ,” a reminder and provision for travelers, giving the kindled fire a useful yield unlike the section's failed strike.
Hellfire throws “شَرَرٍ كَالْقَصْرِ,” an abundance of sparks that reverses the section's “hayyāb,” the striker that produces none.
The next ayah compares the sparks to “جِمَالَتٌ صُفْرٌ,” extending their scale and abundance against the sparkless striker.
The lamp's oil “يَكَادُ زَيْتُهَا يُضِيءُ وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نَارٌ,” a specific image of near self-emitting light opposite the hand left without a spark.
In layered darkness a person can hardly see his hand, and “مَن لَّمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُورًا فَمَا لَهُ مِن نُّورٍ”; this parallels the section's hand left without light.
A deed is likened to a smooth rock covered in soil, which a downpour leaves bare; the visible covering and lost yield parallel a deed that leaves its doer with nothing.
“رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم” pictures what people earned as a rusting cover over their hearts, an inward darkening that parallels the section's self made dim by suppression.
Those who “يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُمْ” are checked by “بَلِ اللَّهُ يُزَكِّي مَن يَشَاءُ”; this sets a boundary on reading 91:9's purification as self-asserted achievement.
“فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنفُسَكُمْ” warns against claiming one's own purity, qualifying the section's language of purifying the self with God's knowledge of who is truly mindful.
The verse says that without God's grace none would be purified and that “اللَّهَ يُزَكِّي مَن يَشَاءُ”; this makes divine agency a boundary around the section's success through purification.
“إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْتَرُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ الْكَذِبَ لَا يُفْلِحُونَ” explicitly joins fabricated falsehood to failure, repeating the connection in 20:61.
At the weighing, those whose scales are heavy “هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ”; this makes success a measured outcome, relevant to the section's shrinking or preserved share.
The light-scaled are said to have lost themselves, “خَسِرُوا أَنفُسَهُم,” the explicit opposite of the successful heavy-scaled in 7:8 and a concrete loss of self.
After prayer, people are told to seek God's bounty and remember Him “لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ”; seeking, effort, and the desired success are stated together.
Moses asks Pharaoh “هَل لَّكَ إِلَىٰ أَن تَزَكَّىٰ”; the same purification verb is an invitation to the transgressor, making purification a chosen response to wrongdoing.
The next verse offers guidance to the Lord and fear of Him, “وَأَهْدِيَكَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَتَخْشَىٰ,” completing the invitation to purify in 79:18.
The gardens of Eden, abiding forever, are “جَزَاءُ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ”; this directly joins purification to an enduring good outcome.
The charity is taken “تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم بِهَا,” cleansing and purifying the giver; this specifies a deed through which the section's tazkiya is realized.
The blind man who comes may “يَزَّكَّىٰ”; the section's purification is joined to a seeker who arrives for a reminder.
The next verse says he may remember and benefit from the reminder, “أَوْ يَذَّكَّرُ فَتَنفَعَهُ الذِّكْرَىٰ,” joining purification to the section's rememberer who fears.
The counterfigure “مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ” considers himself self-sufficient; this anticipates the section's failed, self-diminishing course and the contrast in 92:8.
The speaker gives attention to that self-sufficient man, “فَأَنتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّىٰ,” while the seeker in 80:8–9 is the one who comes striving and fearing.
“If he does not purify himself” (“أَلَّا يَزَّكَّىٰ”) is set against the eager seeker; it makes the failure to purify an explicit boundary, not a lack of opportunity.
The other person “جَاءَكَ يَسْعَىٰ,” comes striving; this directly stages the search and effort in the section's image.
He also “وَهُوَ يَخْشَىٰ,” matching the fearful recipient of reminder in 87:10.
The striving, fearful seeker is turned away from, “فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّىٰ”; this reverses the welcome given to the self-sufficient figure in 80:5–6 and echoes the avoided reminder in 87:11.
Abraham asks for a messenger who will recite, teach, and “يُزَكِّيهِمْ”; this shows purification as a gift mediated to people, alongside the section's account of a person purifying the self.
The messenger's mission includes “وَيُزَكِّيكُمْ,” a direct instance of the same purification root with God and messenger as agents rather than the individual as agent.
The messenger sent among believers “وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ”; this repeats the section's purification theme while specifying its communal, prophetic agent.
The unlettered are taught and purified by the messenger, “وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ”; the verse supplies the same root in a communal form, distinct from the individual's self-purification in 91:9.
Repentance, faith, and good work are followed by hope of being “مِنَ الْمُفْلِحِينَ”; this names a concrete route to the success the section ties to purification.

In the parable, foam from both floodwater and smelted metal is cast away, while what benefits people remains on earth; this closely stages the section's distinction between lasting good and a fruitless yield.

The next verse contrasts those who respond to God and receive the best with those who refuse and face a bad reckoning and Hell; it supplies the moral outcomes after 13:17's image of what remains and what is discarded.
The person who seeks the immediate life receives only what is willed for him, while Hell is the end prepared for him; this directly asks what the seeker actually gets.
The one who seeks the Hereafter, strives for it with faith, has an effort that is appreciated; this is a specific counterpart to the section's successful search.
The following verse says that both groups receive provision from their Lord in this life, qualifying the idea of success by distinguishing immediate provision from the final outcome in 17:18–19.
The passage says the Hereafter is greater in rank and distinction than this life, directly extending the near-life versus lasting-good contrast in 87:16–17.
The worldly-life parable grows green, then dries and becomes scattered debris; beside the lasting good deeds of 18:46, it contrasts what vanishes with what remains.
The question about the greatest losers in deeds introduces people whose effort fails despite their confidence; the next verse supplies the section's specific parallel of a search that yields no good.
Their effort has gone astray in worldly life although they think they are doing well, a precise case of striving without attaining the sought good.
The next verse says their deeds are null and have no weight on the Day of Resurrection, completing the failed effort described in 18:104.
The verse states that wrongdoers are recompensed for their deeds and good-doers receive the best; it grounds the purification warning of 53:32 in the section's two different outcomes.
The passage singles out one who turns away; this gives a concrete act of avoidance alongside the section's account of the ashqa who avoids a reminder.
That person gives a little and then withholds, a specific image of the stinginess opposite the giving and purification in 92:18 and the self-sufficient course in 92:8.
Each soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow and to fear God; this makes the section's question of what each seeker gains an explicit self-accounting.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, a direct image of the self-neglect that the section calls dimming and diminishing the soul.
The continuation after the great fire of 87:12 says its inhabitants neither die nor live, completing the lasting consequence for the ashqa who avoids reminder.
Immediately after the division into wretched and happy in 11:105, the wretched are assigned to the Fire; the verse gives the first concrete outcome of the section's sh-q-w root.
The next verse describes their continued stay in the Fire, extending the wretched outcome from 11:106.
The happy are placed in the Garden and remain there; this completes the contrast introduced by the wretched and happy in 11:105 and makes lasting good concrete.
After confessing that their wretchedness overcame them in 23:106, the people ask to be taken out of the Fire so they can do good; the desired return is now unavailable.
They are told to remain there in humiliation and not speak, completing the failed plea of 23:107.
After the defiant tyrant has failed in 14:15, the next verse places Hell before him and describes a foul drink, giving that failure a concrete end.
The following verse depicts him barely swallowing, with death approaching from every side but not arriving; his striving ends in unrelieved affliction.
After 20:111 says the bearer of wrongdoing has failed, this verse gives the opposite case: a believer doing good need fear neither injustice nor loss.
The “tranquil soul” is a clear counter-image to the section's dimmed and diminished self.
The tranquil soul returns to its Lord both pleased and pleasing, giving the purified self a specific satisfied end.
The next verse invites that soul among God's servants, continuing its welcome after the return in 89:28.
The passage ends by admitting the soul to the Garden, the lasting good that contrasts with the section's failed outcome.
A believing man or woman who does good is promised a good life and reward according to the best of their work, concretely connecting good action with what the person receives.
The verse calls the one removed from the Fire and admitted to the Garden successful, defining success as the final outcome opposite to the wretched fire in the section's cross-references.
The righteous say they feed others only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, a close parallel to 92:19–20's account of giving without seeking a return from people.
The righteous are told that their effort has been appreciated as their reward; this states the successful return to effort that the section contrasts with wasted toil.
